charandauruapan-sb: Charanda is the cane spirit of Michoacán, made around Uruapan from sugarcane juice or molasses, and it grew up around the sugar mills the Spanish established in the region. Its name is usually traced to the Cerro de la Charanda, a hill near the city whose Purépecha name is translated as red earth. It has its own Mexican denomination of origin, which ties it to a group of municipalities in Michoacán, and this bottling carries the name of Uruapan itself.
pitorrocasero-sb: Pitorro is Puerto Rico's moonshine: rum distilled at home, outside the licensed trade, from cane, molasses or sugar, and often steeped with fruit or spices once it comes off the still. It is closely tied to the island's Christmas season, when homemade bottles circulate at parrandas, the musical visits that move from house to house. Nobody is credited with inventing it and the origin of the word pitorro is not documented. Casero simply means homemade, which is how most pitorro has always been made.
patronsilver-sb: Patrón was founded in 1989 by John Paul DeJoria and Martin Crowley, who set out to sell a premium, 100 per cent blue agave tequila in the United States at a time when much of the tequila sold there was mixto. The first bottles were made at the Siete Leguas distillery in Atotonilco el Alto, in the Jalisco highlands, until the brand moved production to its own distillery in 2002. Patrón is Spanish for boss. Silver, the unaged expression, sits at the centre of the range, and Bacardi bought the company in 2018.
patronreposado-sb: Patrón Reposado comes from the company John Paul DeJoria and Martin Crowley founded in 1989 to sell premium highland tequila in the United States. The spirit is now made at Hacienda Patrón in Atotonilco el Alto, Jalisco, where cooked agave is crushed both by a stone tahona and by a roller mill and the two are blended. The reposado rests that spirit in oak for a few months, which places it between the unaged Silver and the Añejo. Until 2002 Patrón was distilled under contract at the nearby Siete Leguas distillery.
patronanejo-sb: Patrón Añejo belongs to the range begun in 1989 by John Paul DeJoria and Martin Crowley, who wanted to sell American drinkers a costly sipping tequila rather than a mixer. The añejo is aged for more than a year in oak at Hacienda Patrón in Atotonilco el Alto, in the Jalisco highlands, and like the rest of the range it goes into heavy glass bottles with a numbered label. The spirit was first made at the Siete Leguas distillery before Patrón opened its own, and Bacardi has owned the brand since 2018.
donjulioblanco-sb: The tequila bearing Don Julio González's name dates, the brand says, to 1985, when his sons created it to mark his sixtieth birthday. He had begun distilling in 1942, at seventeen, at his La Primavera distillery in Atotonilco el Alto in the Jalisco highlands, and had sold his earlier tequila under the Tres Magueyes name. The squat Don Julio bottle is often said to have been designed so guests could see one another across the table, and Diageo has owned the brand outright since 2014.
donjulio1942-sb: Don Julio González began making tequila in 1942, when he was seventeen, at a distillery in Atotonilco el Alto in the Jalisco highlands, and this añejo is named for that year. It came long after the Don Julio brand itself, which his sons created in 1985 to mark his sixtieth birthday, and it is aged for at least two and a half years in American oak. Its tall, narrow bottle set it apart from the squat Don Julio bottle, and the brand has belonged to Diageo outright since 2014.
donjulio70cristalino-sb: Don Julio 70 was released in the early 2010s to mark seventy years since Don Julio González began making tequila in 1942, and the brand bills it as the first añejo claro: a tequila aged like an añejo and then filtered through charcoal to strip out the colour while keeping much of the barrel's flavour. It helped popularise the cristalino style, which many other houses have since taken up. The tequila is made in Atotonilco el Alto, in the Jalisco highlands, under Diageo's ownership.
herraduraplata-sb: Casa Herradura dates to 1870, when Félix López registered the agave fields and distillery of the Hacienda San José del Refugio in Amatitán, Jalisco, as a tequila producer. The name means horseshoe, and company lore says Aurelio López found one gleaming like gold in the agave fields and kept it for luck. The ruins of the hacienda's nineteenth-century distillery still stand beside the working one, and Brown-Forman has owned Herradura since 2007.
herradurareposado-sb: Herradura says it introduced the reposado style in 1974, resting tequila in oak for a matter of months, a halfway point between blanco and añejo that later became one of tequila's main legal categories. The house itself dates to 1870, when Félix López registered the Hacienda San José del Refugio in Amatitán, Jalisco, as a tequila producer, and it takes its name from a horseshoe that, the story goes, was found glinting in the agave fields. It is still made at the hacienda, which Brown-Forman bought in 2007.
fortalezablanco-sb: Fortaleza was launched in 2005 by Guillermo Erickson Sauza, great-great-grandson of Cenobio Sauza, decades after his family had sold the Sauza brand. He brought back into use a small distillery on the family's old estate in the town of Tequila and returned to the slow methods it was built for: brick ovens, a stone tahona to crush the cooked agave, and copper pot stills. In Mexico the tequila is sold as Los Abuelos, the grandfathers, while elsewhere it carries the distillery's name, which means the fortress.
fortalezareposado-sb: Fortaleza Reposado comes from the small distillery in the town of Tequila that Guillermo Erickson Sauza, a descendant of the Sauza tequila family, revived and relaunched in 2005. The agave is cooked in brick ovens, crushed by a stone tahona and distilled twice in copper pot stills, and the reposado then rests in American oak for several months. Each bottle is hand-blown and closed with a stopper shaped like a cooked agave heart, and in Mexico the tequila is sold as Los Abuelos, the grandfathers.
ochoplata-sb: Tequila Ocho was founded in 2008 by Carlos Camarena, of the family that runs La Alteña distillery in Arandas, and Tomas Estes, a restaurateur who did much to bring tequila to European bars. Their idea was to treat agave the way winemakers treat grapes: each batch comes from a single named field, or rancho, and the label records the field and the year, so no two releases are quite the same. Ocho is Spanish for eight. The plata is bottled unaged so those differences between fields show clearly.
tapatio110-sb: Tapatío is the original brand of La Alteña, the distillery Don Felipe Camarena founded in 1937 in the highlands around Arandas, Jalisco, and still run by his family; his grandson Carlos Camarena became its master distiller. For decades the tequila was sold almost entirely in Mexico before it reached export markets. Tapatío is the nickname for someone from Guadalajara or, more broadly, Jalisco. The 110 is the blanco bottled at 110 proof, or 55 per cent, rather than at the usual 40.
eltesoroanejo-sb: El Tesoro de Don Felipe was created in the late 1980s at La Alteña, the Arandas distillery Felipe Camarena founded in 1937, and its name, Don Felipe's treasure, honours him. The Camarena family developed it with the American importer Robert Denton, who wanted a highland tequila made in the old way, with a stone tahona and copper pot stills. The brand now belongs to Suntory Global Spirits, while the Camarena family still makes it at La Alteña.
casamigosblanco-sb: Casamigos began as a private tequila that George Clooney, Rande Gerber and Mike Meldman had made for themselves in 2011, after years spent together at their homes in Mexico; in 2013 they turned it into a company and began selling it to the public. The name joins the Spanish words casa and amigos, house of friends. It is produced in Jalisco, and the blanco is the expression the brand was built on. Diageo bought Casamigos in 2017.
claseazulreposado-sb: Clase Azul was founded in Mexico in 1997 by Arturo Lomelí, who set out to pair tequila with Mexican craft. Its reposado, the brand's flagship, comes in a tall white ceramic decanter painted with blue designs, each one shaped and hand-painted by artisans, many of them from Mazahua communities in central Mexico. The tequila inside is a reposado from Jalisco, rested in oak for several months, and the decanter has become as much the point of the brand as the spirit it holds.
espolonblanco-sb: Espolòn was launched in 1998 by master distiller Cirilo Oropeza, who had begun building the Casa San Nicolás distillery in the Los Altos highlands of Jalisco two years earlier. The name is the spur on the back of a rooster's leg, and a rooster called Ramón appears on the labels, whose artwork draws on the prints of the Mexican engraver José Guadalupe Posada. The brand now belongs to Campari, and Oropeza remained its master distiller until his death in 2020.
olmecaaltosplata-sb: Olmeca Altos was created at the end of the 2000s by two London bartenders, Henry Besant and Dre Masso, working with master distiller Jesús Hernández, to give bars a reasonably priced 100 per cent agave tequila. The name refers to Los Altos, the highlands of Jalisco around Arandas, where the agave is grown and the spirit is made, part of it crushed by a traditional stone tahona. It belongs to Pernod Ricard, which also owns the older Olmeca brand whose name it shares.
cazadoresreposado-sb: Tequila Cazadores dates its recipe to 1922, when, the brand says, José María Bañuelos developed it in Arandas, in the highlands of Jalisco; the tequila went on general sale only decades later. The name means hunters, and a stag stands on the label. The house built its reputation on reposado, rested in American oak for a few months, which remains its signature expression. Bacardi has owned the brand since 2002 and still makes it in Arandas.
josecuervotradicional-sb: Jose Cuervo's history as a tequila maker begins in 1795, when José María Guadalupe de Cuervo received a royal licence from Carlos IV of Spain to produce vino mezcal in the town of Tequila, Jalisco, on land his father had been granted decades earlier. The family's La Rojeña distillery, established in 1812, is often called the oldest working distillery in Latin America. Tradicional is the house's 100 per cent blue agave reposado, and the company is still controlled by the Beckmann family, descendants of the founders.
1800anejo-sb: The Beckmann family, owners of Jose Cuervo, launched this brand in the late 1960s, by most accounts, as a sipping tequila to stand above their everyday labels, and the añejo was its first expression, sold at first under the Cuervo name. The brand name refers to the year eighteen hundred, which the brand gives as the point when tequila was first aged in oak. It is still made in Jalisco by the Cuervo company.
sieteleguasblanco-sb: Siete Leguas was founded in 1952 by Ignacio González Vargas in Atotonilco el Alto, in the highlands of Jalisco, and is named after the horse of the revolutionary general Pancho Villa; siete leguas means seven leagues. The González family still runs it, from two distilleries, one of which still crushes agave with a stone tahona. For years it also made the tequila sold under the Patrón name, until that brand moved to its own distillery in 2002. The blanco is the house's unaged expression.
g4blanco-sb: G4 is made at El Pandillo, the distillery Felipe Camarena, a member of the Camarena tequila family, built in the early 2010s in the Jalisco highlands near Jesús María. He is known for engineering his own equipment, including a mechanical stone crusher nicknamed Frankenstein, and for making tequila with a blend of collected rainwater and spring water. The brand says the name stands for four generations of the family in tequila. The blanco is unaged, bottled to show off the agave and the water.
chinacoanejo-sb: Chinaco comes from González, in Tamaulipas, one of the few places far from Jalisco inside the tequila denomination, where Guillermo González Díaz Lombardo planted agave and built the La Gonzaleña distillery. In 1983 it became, by most accounts, the first 100 per cent agave tequila imported into the United States, brought in by Robert Denton and Marilyn Smith. The name recalls the chinacos, horsemen who fought the French intervention in nineteenth-century Mexico. Production stopped for some years before the distillery reopened.
delmagueyvida-sb: Del Maguey was founded in 1995 by the American artist Ron Cooper, who had come to know family mezcal makers in Oaxaca and began bottling each village's mezcal separately under the name Single Village Mezcal. Vida was added later as a mezcal meant for mixing, made from espadín agave cooked in earthen pits and distilled in small stills by a family producer in the village of San Luis del Río. Its name is Spanish for life. Pernod Ricard became the majority owner of Del Maguey in 2017.
delmagueychichicapa-sb: Chichicapa is one of the early Single Village mezcals that the American artist Ron Cooper bottled after founding Del Maguey in 1995, each labelled with the village where it was made rather than with a blend name. It comes from San Baltazar Chichicapam, in the Oaxacan hills, where a family producer roasts espadín in an earthen pit, crushes it with a stone wheel drawn by an animal and distils it twice in a small still. Putting the village on the label was Cooper's way of crediting the place and the maker.
delmagueytobala-sb: Tobalá is the local name for Agave potatorum, a small wild agave that grows at high altitude in the Oaxacan mountains, often in the shade of oak trees, and that is gathered rather than farmed. Each plant yields little, which has always made tobalá mezcal scarce. Del Maguey, founded in 1995 by the American artist Ron Cooper to bottle the mezcals of individual Oaxacan villages, includes a tobalá made by one of its family producers from wild-gathered plants.
delmagueypechuga-sb: Pechuga is a celebration mezcal from Oaxaca: an already distilled mezcal is run through the still a third time with wild fruits, nuts, rice and spices, while a raw chicken breast, the pechuga that gives the style its name, hangs in the still in the path of the vapours. It was traditionally made in small amounts for weddings, feast days and the end-of-year holidays, when the fruit is in season. Del Maguey, founded by the artist Ron Cooper in 1995, bottles its pechuga from one of its family producers.
ilegaljoven-sb: Ilegal began in 2004 at Café No Sé, the bar the American John Rexer ran in Antigua, Guatemala, where he served mezcal he brought in informally from Oaxaca, and in 2006 he turned it into a brand named for those unofficial beginnings. The mezcal is made from espadín by the Hernández family at their Mal de Amor distillery in Santiago Matatlán, Oaxaca. Bacardi took a minority stake in 2015 and bought the company outright in 2023, and Joven is the unaged expression.
ilegalreposado-sb: Ilegal Reposado comes from the brand John Rexer started in 2006, after two years of informally bringing Oaxacan mezcal into Guatemala for Café No Sé, his bar in Antigua; the name recalls those unofficial shipments. The mezcal is distilled from espadín by the Hernández family at their Mal de Amor distillery in Santiago Matatlán, Oaxaca, and the reposado is then rested for a few months in American oak, which softens the smoke. Bacardi has owned the brand outright since 2023.
montelobosespadin-sb: Montelobos was created in the early 2010s by Iván Saldaña, a Mexican biologist who had studied agave scientifically, with the spirits company Casa Lumbre. It is distilled in Santiago Matatlán, Oaxaca, from organically grown espadín roasted in an earthen pit before fermentation, and its name means wolf mountain. Saldaña has also written a book on the science of agave spirits, and the brand presents itself as a bridge between that research and traditional mezcal making.
mezcalvagoelote-sb: Mezcal Vago was founded in 2013 by the American Judah Kuper and partners together with Aquilino García López, a mezcalero in Candelaria Yegolé, Oaxaca, whose daughter Kuper married. Elote began as Aquilino's mezcal: espadín redistilled with corn grown on his farm and toasted, a nod to the maize that grows alongside agave in Oaxacan fields. The brand has since added mezcals from several other family producers, each named on the label.
reycamperotepeztate-sb: Rey Campero is made by the Sánchez Parada family in Candelaria Yegolé, in Oaxaca's southern sierra, a village where they have distilled mezcal for generations, and Rómulo Sánchez Parada began bottling it under the Rey Campero name, king of the countryside, in the early 2010s. Tepeztate, Agave marmorata, is a wild agave that grows on steep, rocky slopes and can take a quarter of a century to mature, so the family gathers it rather than plants it, and each batch depends on what the hills provide.
bozalcuishe-sb: Cuishe is a wild Oaxacan agave of the karwinskii group, which also includes madrecuixe, barril and tobasiche, and its tall, narrow trunk gives a dry, herbal mezcal. It is gathered from hillsides rather than farmed, and like other mezcals it is roasted in an earthen pit before fermentation and distillation. Bozal bottles it as a single-agave mezcal, made from cuishe alone.
losamantesjoven-sb: Los Amantes, the lovers, is an unaged joven mezcal from Oaxaca, the state that makes most of Mexico's mezcal.
alipussanandres-sb: Alipús is a line of village mezcals created by the team behind Los Danzantes, a Oaxacan restaurant group that also runs its own distillery in Santiago Matatlán. Rather than blending, each Alipús bottling comes from a single family producer and carries the name of the village where it is made; San Andrés is one of them, an espadín mezcal from the Oaxacan hills. The idea, shared with other single-village labels, is to bring the work of small palenques to a wider market while keeping each maker's style intact.
bacanoracielorojo-sb: Bacanora is the agave spirit of Sonora, named for the town of Bacanora in the foothills of the Sierra Madre and distilled from wild Agave angustifolia. Families in the sierra made it for generations, but the state outlawed its production for most of the twentieth century, so it survived as a clandestine spirit until it was legalised again late in the century and later given its own denomination of origin. Cielo Rojo, red sky, is one of the brands bottled since legalisation.
sotolporsiempre-sb: Sotol is distilled in Chihuahua, Durango and Coahuila from the desert spoon, a Dasylirion plant that looks like an agave but is not one, and it takes years to mature in the wild. Rural families of the Chihuahuan Desert have made it for generations, roasting the plant hearts in pits much as mezcal makers do, and it now has a Mexican denomination of origin covering those three states. Por Siempre, meaning forever, is a sotol bottled in that tradition.
raicillalavenenosa-sb: Raicilla comes from western Jalisco, from the coast around Cabo Corrientes and the mountains around Mascota, where it is distilled from local agaves such as maximiliana and angustifolia. The name means little root, and the usual story is that producers called it that in colonial times to avoid the taxes levied on mezcal. La Venenosa, the poisonous one, was started by Esteban Morales to bottle raicillas from individual traditional makers, each labelled with its region and its maestro.
comitecobaluncanan-sb: Comiteco is the traditional spirit of Comitán de Domínguez in Chiapas, distilled from fermented agave sap, the aguamiel also used for pulque, often with cane sugar or piloncillo added to the ferment. It has been made in the Comitán area since colonial times. Balún Canán is the old Maya name for Comitán, usually translated as nine stars or nine guardians, and it is also the title of Rosario Castellanos's novel set in the town.
cocuypecayero-sb: Cocuy is the agave spirit of northwestern Venezuela, distilled in the states of Falcón and Lara from Agave cocui, whose hearts are roasted in pits much as in Mexican mezcal. For long stretches of the twentieth century much of it was made clandestinely, outside the law, by rural families. Pecayero means from Pecaya, a town in Falcón whose cocuy received a Venezuelan denomination of origin, and the name marks this bottling as coming from that tradition.
hennessyvs-sb: Hennessy was founded in 1765 by Richard Hennessy, an Irish officer who had served in the French army under Louis XV and settled in Cognac, where he began distilling and exporting brandy. The house introduced star ratings on its labels in 1865, and its youngest blend, long sold as Three Star, is today labelled VS, very special, meaning its youngest eau-de-vie has spent at least two years in oak. Hennessy merged with Moët et Chandon in 1971, and the group became part of LVMH in 1987.
hennessyvsop-sb: Hennessy says the VSOP grade began in 1817, when the Prince Regent of Britain, the future George IV, asked the house for a very superior old pale cognac. The house had been founded in Cognac in 1765 by Richard Hennessy, an Irish officer in the French army, and the initials it adopted became the standard for cognac aged at least four years in oak. Pale is usually explained as meaning cognac sold without added caramel colouring. Hennessy is now part of LVMH, through Moët Hennessy.
hennessyxo-sb: Maurice Hennessy created XO, extra old, in 1870, at first as a cognac for his family and friends, and the house says it was the first to carry those letters, which later became an official grade for cognac with long ageing. He was a descendant of Richard Hennessy, the Irish officer who founded the house in Cognac in 1765. The blend draws on old eaux-de-vie from several crus, and Hennessy is now part of LVMH, through Moët Hennessy.
remymartinvsop-sb: Rémy Martin VSOP was popularised from 1927 by André Renaud, a partner in the house, who built it around Fine Champagne, a blend of eaux-de-vie from Grande and Petite Champagne, the two most prized crus, with at least half from Grande Champagne. The house had been founded in 1724 by Rémy Martin, a winegrower from near Rouillac, and later adopted a centaur, the zodiac sign of Paul-Émile Rémy Martin, as its emblem. Rémy Martin merged with Cointreau in 1990 to form Rémy Cointreau.
remymartinxo-sb: Rémy Martin XO was created in 1981 by the house's cellar master André Giraud as a richer, older blend than the VSOP that had made the brand's name, and it draws on as many as four hundred eaux-de-vie. Like everything Rémy Martin makes, it is a Fine Champagne cognac, made only from Grande and Petite Champagne grapes. The house dates to 1724, when Rémy Martin, a winegrower, began trading cognac, and its centaur emblem comes from the star sign of a later head of the family.
remymartinlouisxiii-sb: Louis XIII was created in 1874 by Paul-Émile Rémy Martin, who named it in homage to the seventeenth-century French king. It is a blend of very old eaux-de-vie from Grande Champagne alone, many of them aged for decades, and it is sold in a crystal decanter modelled, the house says, on a metal flask found on the site of the sixteenth-century Battle of Jarnac. Each cellar master lays down eaux-de-vie for it that only a successor will use, so every bottle spans several generations of the house's work.
martellvs-sb: Martell was founded in 1715 by Jean Martell, a merchant from Jersey who began trading brandy on the banks of the Charente at Cognac, and it is usually counted the oldest of the great cognac houses. The house came to lean on the Borderies, a small cru prized for floral eaux-de-vie, and on fine-grained oak from the Tronçais forest. VS is its youngest blend. Seagram bought Martell in 1987, and Pernod Ricard has owned it since 2001.
martellcordonbleu-sb: Édouard Martell created Cordon Bleu in 1912, nearly two centuries after his ancestor Jean Martell, a merchant from Jersey, founded the house in Cognac in 1715. It was built around eaux-de-vie from the Borderies, the smallest cognac cru, which give it a floral, nutty character, and it is widely credited as the first premium cognac sold on a large scale. Martell has belonged to Pernod Ricard since 2001.
courvoisiervsop-sb: Courvoisier grew from a wine and spirits business that Emmanuel Courvoisier and Louis Gallois ran at Bercy, then just outside Paris, which Napoleon is recorded visiting in 1811. A legend that he took cognac from the house with him into exile on St Helena gave Courvoisier its old slogan, the cognac of Napoleon. Félix Courvoisier and Jules Gallois later moved the business to Jarnac, in the Cognac region, where it is still based. The Campari Group bought Courvoisier in 2024.
camusvsop-sb: Camus was founded in 1863 by Jean-Baptiste Camus, a winegrower who gathered a group of growers to sell their cognac under a shared brand he called La Grande Marque. It has stayed with the same family for five generations, now led by Cyril Camus, and remains independent. The family's base is the Borderies, the smallest of the cognac crus, and the house's cognacs, its VSOP included, draw on that area's rich, floral eaux-de-vie.
delamainpaledryxo-sb: Delamain dates its house to 1824 and traces its roots to James Delamain, an Irishman who had joined the cognac trade in Jarnac in the eighteenth century. Unusually, the house distils nothing itself: it selects old Grande Champagne eaux-de-vie from growers and ages them in its own cellars on the Charente. Pale and Dry shows the lighter, drier style of old cognac that has become the house's signature, and Delamain now belongs to the Bollinger family group.
frapinvsop-sb: The Frapin family has grown vines in Grande Champagne, the most prized cognac cru, since the thirteenth century, according to the house, and it has long been based at Segonzac, at the heart of that cru. Unlike most large houses, Frapin makes its cognac only from grapes grown on its own estate, and it distils and ages the eaux-de-vie on the property. Its VSOP is therefore a single-estate Grande Champagne cognac, a rarer thing than the blended cognacs that dominate the trade.
pierreferrand1840-sb: This cognac was introduced in the early 2010s by Alexandre Gabriel, owner of the Ferrand estate in Grande Champagne, working with the drinks historian David Wondrich. They modelled it on a bottle of 1840 cognac from the house of Pinet Castillon, aiming for the strong, fruity style that nineteenth-century bartenders such as Jerry Thomas would have mixed into punches and juleps. It is bottled at a higher strength than most cognac for that reason, and the name points to the year of the bottle that inspired it.
darrozelesgrandsassemblages-sb: Darroze is the work of Francis Darroze, whose family ran a well-known restaurant in Villeneuve-de-Marsan in the Landes, and who in the 1970s began seeking out armagnacs from individual small estates, buying and ageing them himself and bottling each under the name of its property. His son Marc Darroze runs the house today. Les Grands Assemblages are its blended range, labelled by age, made by marrying eaux-de-vie from several of those estates rather than from a single one.
chateaudelaubadevsop-sb: Château de Laubade is a Bas-Armagnac estate at Sorbets, in the Gers, which the Lesgourgues family has owned since the 1970s. Unusually for a large armagnac house, it grows its own grapes on the estate's vineyards and distils them in its own continuous armagnac still, then ages the spirit in Gascon oak. Bas-Armagnac, the westernmost of the three armagnac districts, is known for sandy soils and fine, fruity brandies, and the VSOP is the estate's younger blend.
delord25-sb: Delord began with Prosper Delord, a travelling distiller who moved between farms with a mobile still, distilling armagnac for growers; the family dates its own house to 1893 and settled at Lannepax, in the Gers. The Delords still distil with old armagnac stills and age their spirit in their cellars there, now several generations on. Delord 25 is a blend whose youngest eau-de-vie has spent at least twenty-five years in oak, showing how armagnac changes over very long ageing.
boulardgrandsolage-sb: Boulard was founded in 1825 by Pierre-Auguste Boulard in the Pays d'Auge, the Normandy district whose calvados must be double distilled in pot stills, and it became one of the region's best-known houses. Its cellars at Coquainvilliers age apple brandy in oak casks of many sizes. Grand Solage is the house's blend of young and older calvados, made to be approachable while keeping the cider-apple character of the region, and calvados itself is distilled from cider pressed from local apples and pears.
peremagloirevsop-sb: Père Magloire is a calvados house based in the Pays d'Auge, the Normandy district that gives the appellation its most closely regulated apple brandy, and it dates its name to 1821. Calvados is distilled from cider made from local apples and sometimes pears and then aged in oak, and a VSOP must have spent at least four years in wood.
christiandrouinselection-sb: The Drouin calvados house began in 1960, when Christian Drouin senior bought a farm at Gonneville-sur-Honfleur in the Pays d'Auge, and his son Christian went on to sell the farm's calvados under the family name. The family still ages the apple brandy in old casks on the estate, now in the third generation under Guillaume Drouin. Sélection is the house's youngest calvados, with around two years in oak, and keeps the fresh cider-apple character that the older bottlings round out.
massenezpoirewilliams-sb: Massenez is an Alsatian fruit-brandy house founded in the late nineteenth century in the Villé valley, where the region's orchards have long supplied distillers of eau-de-vie. Poire Williams is a clear brandy distilled from the Williams pear, the variety called Bartlett in North America, and Alsatian houses made it a speciality. Massenez is known for selling it with a whole pear inside the bottle, grown there by slipping the bottle over the young fruit on the tree and leaving it until harvest.
massenezkirsch-sb: Kirsch, short for Kirschwasser, cherry water, is a clear brandy distilled from fermented small black cherries, stones included, in the Black Forest, Alsace and Switzerland. Massenez, founded in the Villé valley of Alsace in the late nineteenth century, is among the Alsatian houses that made fruit brandy their whole business. Its kirsch is unaged and colourless, as the style traditionally is, with the faint almond note that comes from the cherry stones.
marcdebourgogne-sb: Marc de Bourgogne is the pomace brandy of Burgundy, distilled from the skins, pips and stems left after the region's grapes have been pressed for wine, and its name comes from marc, the French word for that pressed residue. Growers once distilled it on the estate or with travelling stills, as a way to make use of the pomace. It differs from Italian grappa in usually being aged in oak, which gives it an amber colour and a rounder, earthier character, and it is now a protected geographical indication.
torres10-sb: Torres began making brandy in 1928, when Juan Torres Casals, second generation of a Penedès wine family, started distilling wine in Vilafranca del Penedès, in Catalonia. The business had been founded in 1870 by the brothers Jaime and Miguel Torres; Jaime had made his fortune in Cuba before returning home to go into wine with his brother. Torres 10 is a Gran Reserva brandy aged in oak, made in Catalonia, far from the sherry country of Jerez.
cardenalmendoza-sb: Cardenal Mendoza was first produced in 1887 by Sánchez Romate, a Jerez house founded in 1781, and it is named after Pedro González de Mendoza, the fifteenth-century cardinal who advised the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand and Isabella. It is a Brandy de Jerez Solera Gran Reserva, aged in casks that previously held sherry, mainly oloroso and Pedro Ximénez, moving through a solera so that younger brandy is blended with older. It remains one of the most widely known Spanish brandies.
lepanto-sb: Lepanto is the brandy of González Byass, the Jerez sherry house founded in 1835 by Manuel María González, later joined by his English agent Robert Blake Byass. It is named after the naval battle of Lepanto, fought in 1571. It is one of the few Brandies de Jerez distilled by the house itself, in copper pot stills, from Palomino wine grown around Jerez, before ageing by solera in casks that held the house's sherries.
orujodegalicia-sb: Orujo de Galicia is the pomace brandy of northwestern Spain, distilled from the skins and pips left after winemaking, and its name comes from orujo, the Spanish word for that residue. Galician families long distilled it at home in small copper stills, sometimes with the help of travelling distillers, and it is now a protected geographical indication. It is the base of queimada, a hot drink of orujo, sugar, lemon peel and coffee beans set alight in a clay bowl while a spell against evil spirits is recited, a ritual whose ancient pedigree is disputed.
nardinigrappa-sb: Nardini was founded in 1779 by Bortolo Nardini, who bought an inn at the end of the wooden bridge over the Brenta in Bassano del Grappa and began distilling there, and the Grapperia Nardini on the bridge is still open. It is often described as the oldest grappa distillery in Italy, and it is still run by the Nardini family. The house is known above all for clear, unaged grappa bottled at fifty per cent, the style it has made since its early days in the Veneto.
polisarpa-sb: Poli was founded in 1898 by GioBatta Poli in Schiavon, in the Veneto, where he began distilling grappa, and the family still runs it, now under Jacopo Poli. Sarpa is the Venetian dialect word for grape pomace, and this grappa is distilled from the pomace of merlot and cabernet in the family's copper pot stills. Jacopo Poli also founded a museum of grappa in nearby Bassano del Grappa, devoted to the history of the spirit and its stills.
noninoilmerlot-sb: In 1973 Benito and Giannola Nonino distilled the pomace of a single grape variety, picolit, on its own, and in doing so are credited with launching the single-varietal grappa that changed how the spirit was regarded in Italy. The family had been distilling at Ronchi di Percoto, in Friuli, since 1897, when Orazio Nonino built the first still. Il Merlot applies the same idea to merlot pomace, distilled in small batches in copper stills. The family also founded the Nonino literary prize in 1975.
vecchiaromagna-sb: Vecchia Romagna comes from the distillery that Jean Bouton, heir to a French distilling family, founded in Bologna in 1820, Italianising his name to Buton. The brand name, old Romagna, was coined in 1939 by Count Achille Sassoli de' Bianchi, after international agreements had reserved the word cognac for France, and the same year brought the triangular bottle that became its signature. Made from Trebbiano grapes, it is one of Italy's most popular brandies and has belonged to the Montenegro group since 1999.
metaxa7star-sb: Spyros Metaxa created his spirit in 1888 in Piraeus, the port of Athens, where he had been running a tavern, and he built a distillery there. The emblem on the bottle, a warrior of Salamis, comes from an ancient medallion said to have been found while the distillery was being built. Metaxa is not legally a brandy: aged grape distillates are blended with sweet Muscat wine from Samos and a secret mix of botanicals, and the stars distinguish its blends.
metaxa12star-sb: Metaxa traces itself to 1888, when Spyros Metaxa, born into a family of silk merchants, began making his spirit in Piraeus and founded a distillery there. His recipe blends aged grape distillates with sweet Muscat wine from Samos and a closely guarded mix of botanicals, which places it outside the legal definition of brandy. The stars distinguish the house's blends, and Grand Metropolitan bought the family company in 1989 before Rémy Cointreau took it over in 2000.
tsipourotirnavou-sb: Tsipouro is the pomace brandy of mainland Greece, distilled from the skins and pips left after winemaking, and tradition credits monks on Mount Athos with making it as early as the fourteenth century, though that story is hard to document. Tyrnavos, in Thessaly, is one of its best-known homes, distilling both plain tsipouro and versions flavoured with anise, and the town marks the autumn distilling season with festivities. Tirnavou simply means of Tyrnavos, which places this bottling in that local tradition.
tsikoudiacrete-sb: Tsikoudia is the pomace brandy of Crete, distilled from the grape skins and pips left after winemaking, and its name is usually traced to tsikouda, the local word for that pressed residue. Every autumn, after the harvest, villages fire up licensed copper stills for a few weeks, and these kazanemata, the distilling days, are social gatherings with food and music. Cretans often call the spirit raki, though it contains no anise, and it is offered chilled in small glasses as a gesture of hospitality.
ararat5-sb: Armenian brandy production began in 1887, when the merchant Nerses Tairyan built a winery and distillery in Yerevan, and the Russian producer Nikolai Shustov bought it at the end of the century. The distillery grew into the Yerevan Brandy Company, and its brandies took the Ararat name, after the mountain that looms over Yerevan. Pernod Ricard bought the company in 1998, and the five-year blend is at the core of its range.
ararat10-sb: Ararat brandies come from the Yerevan Brandy Company, whose history begins in 1887 with Nerses Tairyan's distillery in Yerevan, later run by the Shustov family of Moscow. The brand takes its name from Mount Ararat, the snow-capped peak that dominates the view from the city and is a national symbol of Armenia. The ten-year-old blend is sold as Akhtamar, after an island in Lake Van with a medieval Armenian church, and Pernod Ricard has owned the company since 1998.
zsindelyespalinka-sb: Pálinka is Hungary's fruit brandy, distilled from fermented fruit such as plums, apricots, pears and cherries, with no added sugar or flavouring, and its name is usually traced to a Slavic word for burning. Since Hungary joined the European Union, pálinka has been a protected name reserved for spirits made in Hungary from Hungarian fruit, with apricot pálinka also allowed in four Austrian provinces. Zsindelyes, which means shingled, is the Hungarian producer behind this bottling.
rezangyalpalinka-sb: Rézangyal, copper angel, is a Hungarian pálinka brand whose name evokes the copper stills in which fruit brandy is made. Pálinka is a long-standing tradition of the Carpathian Basin, and EU rules reserve the name for fruit brandy distilled in Hungary from Hungarian fruit, with apricot pálinka also permitted in four Austrian provinces. Hungarian law bans added sugar, colouring and flavouring.
slivovitzjelinek-sb: Rudolf Jelínek is the best-known slivovitz maker in the Czech Republic, based at Vizovice in Moravia, where plum brandy has long been made from the region's orchards, and the firm dates its distilling to 1894. After the Second World War the business was nationalised, and it returned to private hands after the fall of communism. Jelínek is also known abroad for its kosher slivovitz, produced under rabbinical supervision. Slivovitz takes its name from the Slavic word for plum, sliva.
chachaaskaneli-sb: Chacha is Georgia's pomace brandy, distilled from the skins, pips and stems left after winemaking, and chacha is also the Georgian word for that pressed residue. For generations it was made at home in wine villages across the country, especially in Kakheti and western Georgia, and offered with toasts at the supra, the Georgian feast. Askaneli, a Georgian wine and spirits producer, bottles a commercial chacha in that tradition.
piscoporton-sb: Pisco Portón is made at Hacienda La Caravedo in Ica, Peru, a distillery founded in 1684 that is often described as the oldest still working in the Americas. The brand was launched around 2010 with the Peruvian pisco authority Johnny Schuler as its master distiller. Portón means gate. Its piscos follow Peruvian rules: distilled once, to bottling strength, in copper pot stills from fresh grape must, with no water added and no time in wood.
barsolquebranta-sb: BarSol is made at Bodega San Isidro in Ica, on Peru's southern coast, a winery and distillery established in 1919, and the BarSol brand was created in the early 2000s to take Peruvian pisco to export markets. Quebranta is the backbone grape of Peruvian pisco, a non-aromatic variety that arose in Peru from vines the Spanish brought in the sixteenth century, and pisco puro made from it is earthy rather than floral. Like all Peruvian pisco, it is distilled to proof and rests without wood.
capelpisco-sb: Capel is a cooperative of grape growers in Chile's Elqui and Limarí valleys, founded in 1938 at Vicuña, and its name is an abbreviation of its original Spanish title, the agricultural pisco cooperative of Elqui. It grew into one of Chile's largest pisco producers, drawing on the grapes of many small growers. Chile and Peru both claim pisco as a national spirit and dispute the right to the name, and Chilean pisco, unlike Peruvian, may be diluted to strength and aged in wood.
lairdsapplejack-sb: Laird & Company holds what it describes as licence number one, granted in 1780, and it is usually counted the oldest licensed distillery in the United States. The family traces its applejack to William Laird, who came to Monmouth County, New Jersey, from Scotland in 1698, and to Robert Laird, who served under George Washington and is said to have shared the family recipe with him. In colonial times applejack was often concentrated by freezing hard cider and removing the ice, and Laird's now distils in Virginia and bottles in New Jersey.
germainrobin-sb: Germain-Robin was founded in 1982 by Ansley Coale and Hubert Germain-Robin, who had met the year before when Coale, driving near his ranch outside Ukiah in Mendocino County, California, picked up the Frenchman hitchhiking; Germain-Robin's family had made cognac until their business was sold. The two set up a small alembic still on Coale's land and distilled brandy in the cognac manner, but from fine California wine grapes such as pinot noir. E. & J. Gallo bought the business in 2017.
asbachuralt-sb: Hugo Asbach, a native of Cologne, founded his company at Rüdesheim am Rhein on 11 May 1892, and his aged brandy, Asbach Uralt, very old, became the best-known German brandy. After the First World War, when the Treaty of Versailles reserved the name cognac for France, Asbach coined the term Weinbrand for German grape brandy, and it later became the legal name of the category. The town's Rüdesheimer Kaffee, made with the brandy, became a local speciality, and the brand now belongs to Underberg.
kwv10-sb: KWV was founded at Paarl on 8 January 1918 as a cooperative of Cape winegrowers, the Koöperatieve Wijnbouwers Vereniging, to steady prices and raise quality, and for much of the century it regulated South Africa's wine and spirits trade. Brandy had been distilled at the Cape since the Dutch period, and KWV makes its own at its brandy cellar in Worcester. Its 10-year-old is a pot-still brandy, a South African category reserved for brandy made overwhelmingly in pot stills and aged in small oak casks.
cointreau-sb: Cointreau went on sale in 1875, made by the family firm that the confectioner brothers Adolphe and Édouard-Jean Cointreau had founded in Angers in 1849, and Édouard-Jean's son Édouard is usually credited with the recipe of sweet and bitter orange peels distilled with neutral spirit. It was first labelled as a white curaçao triple sec, and the story goes that the family later dropped the term as rivals copied it. The company merged with Rémy Martin in 1990 to form Rémy Cointreau, and the liqueur is still made outside Angers.
grandmarniercordonrouge-sb: Grand Marnier Cordon Rouge was created in 1880 by Louis-Alexandre Marnier-Lapostolle, who had married into a family running a distillery at Neauphle-le-Château since 1827, by blending cognac with an essence of bitter Caribbean oranges and sugar. The hotelier César Ritz is said to have suggested the name, and Marnier-Lapostolle in turn helped him establish the Ritz in Paris. The liqueur became a fixture of French cooking, notably in crêpes Suzette. The Campari Group took over the family company in 2016.
combiertriplesec-sb: Combier was founded in 1834 in Saumur, in the Loire Valley, by Jean-Baptiste Combier, a confectioner, and his wife, who began making a liqueur of bitter orange peels at their shop; the house says it was the first triple sec, a distinction other houses also claim. It is still made in the town, in copper stills more than a century old, from orange peels macerated in alcohol before distillation.
pierreferranddrycuracao-sb: Pierre Ferrand Dry Curaçao was launched in 2012 by Alexandre Gabriel of Maison Ferrand, who developed it with the drinks historian David Wondrich to recreate the drier, brandy-based orange curaçao that nineteenth-century bartenders used, before sweeter versions took over. It is built on bitter orange peels, including the laraha of Curaçao, steeped in brandy and cognac, and it is labelled Ancienne Méthode, old method. Curaçao takes its name from the Caribbean island where the bitter laraha orange grew from Spanish-planted trees.
bolsbluecuracao-sb: Bols dates itself to 1575, when the family opened a small distillery, 't Lootsje, the little shed, in Amsterdam, and it calls itself the oldest distillery brand in the world. Lucas Bols, born in 1652, was a shareholder in the Dutch East India Company, whose ships brought the spices and peels behind the house's liqueurs, and the company says he made a liqueur from the bitter laraha oranges of Curaçao. Bols sold a blue version in 1912 as Crème de Ciel, cream of the sky, and blue became its best-known curaçao.
seniorcuracaoofcuracao-sb: Senior & Co began selling its liqueur from a pharmacy on Curaçao in 1896, and since 1947 it has made it at Landhuis Chobolobo, a colonial manor house in Willemstad. The company bills it as the only curaçao made on the island, from the dried peel of the laraha, a bitter orange descended from the Seville oranges the Spanish planted in 1527, which grew small, bitter and inedible in the dry climate. It sells the same liqueur in several colours, since the colour is added and the flavour stays the same.
stgermain-sb: St-Germain was launched in 2007 by Robert Cooper, son of Norton Cooper of the liqueur house Charles Jacquin et Cie, who had been inspired by elderflower drinks he came across in London. It is made from the blossoms of the elder tree, gathered for a few weeks each spring in the Savoie, in the French Alps, and the brand's story has collectors bringing them down by bicycle. The name comes from the Paris neighbourhood of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and Bacardi bought the brand in 2013.
chambord-sb: Chambord was created in 1982 by Norton Cooper at Charles Jacquin et Cie, inspired by a raspberry liqueur said to have been made in the Loire Valley in the late seventeenth century and served to Louis XIV on his visits to the Château de Chambord, which gives it its name. It is a black raspberry liqueur, made in the Loire Valley from raspberries and blackberries with cognac, vanilla, citrus peel and honey, and its round bottle is modelled on a royal orb. Brown-Forman has owned it since 2006.
lejaycremedecassis-sb: Lejay-Lagoute, in Dijon, credits its founder Auguste-Denis Lagoute with creating crème de cassis in 1841, by steeping Burgundy blackcurrants in alcohol and sweetening the infusion, and the house presents itself as the original maker. Dijon became the capital of the liqueur, and crème de cassis de Bourgogne is now a protected name. After the Second World War the city's mayor, Canon Félix Kir, served white Burgundy with a little cassis at official receptions, and the drink came to bear his name.
giffardcremedeviolette-sb: Giffard was founded in 1885 by Émile Giffard, a pharmacist in Angers who created a mint liqueur, Menthe-Pastille, and turned his pharmacy into a distillery to make it. The family has run the house for four generations since, building a range of liqueurs and syrups that includes this crème de violette, a sweet liqueur flavoured with violet flowers in the old French style. Violet liqueur is the ingredient that gives the Aviation cocktail its pale sky-blue colour.
rothmanwintercremedeviolette-sb: Rothman & Winter Crème de Violette reached the United States in 2007 through the importer Haus Alpenz, at a time when no violet liqueur had been widely available there for decades, and it let bartenders make the Aviation as its original recipe intended. Hugo Ensslin's 1916 recipe for that gin cocktail had called for crème de violette, which later editions often dropped. The liqueur is made in Austria from violets steeped in spirit and sweetened.
tempusfugitcremedementhe-sb: Tempus Fugit Spirits was founded by Peter Schaf and John Troia, two Americans who collected nineteenth-century liqueur bottles and recipes and set out to recreate pre-Prohibition styles that had disappeared from bars. Their crème de menthe, like their crème de cacao, is produced in Switzerland and, the company says, based on a nineteenth-century recipe, made with distilled mint and other botanicals. The company's name is Latin for time flies.
get27-sb: Get 27 was created in 1796 by the brothers Jean and Pierre Get, who began making a peppermint liqueur in Revel, in the Lauragais south-east of Toulouse; their old distillery is now a cultural centre for the town. The 27 originally referred to its strength, though it is now bottled lower, at 21 per cent. Production later moved to Gémenos and, in 1995, to Beaucaire, and the brand now belongs to Bacardi. Its vivid green colour and cool mint flavour made it a familiar sight in French bars, usually served over crushed ice.
luxardomaraschino-sb: Girolamo Luxardo founded his company in 1821 in Zara, now Zadar in Croatia, then part of the Habsburg Kingdom of Dalmatia, after his wife Maria Canevari had made a name with her homemade rosolio maraschino, a liqueur from local marasca cherries. The company distilled the cherries, with their stones and leaves, into a clear liqueur and sold it in straw-wrapped bottles. After the Second World War destroyed the factory, Giorgio Luxardo moved the business to Torreglia, near Padua, where the family grows its own marasca orchards.
luxardolimoncello-sb: Limoncello is the lemon liqueur of southern Italy, made by steeping lemon zest in neutral spirit and sweetening the infusion, and Sorrento, Amalfi and Capri all claim to be its birthplace, each with its own family stories. It was bottled widely for sale only in the late twentieth century. Luxardo, the house Girolamo Luxardo founded in Zara in Dalmatia in 1821 and moved to Torreglia in the Veneto after the Second World War, added a limoncello to a range best known for its maraschino.
pallinilimoncello-sb: Pallini is a Roman family firm founded in 1875 by Nicola Pallini, and it is still run by his descendants. Its limoncello is made from Sfusato Amalfitano lemons, the long, thick-skinned lemon of the Amalfi Coast, whose zest is steeped in spirit and then sweetened. Limoncello's birthplace is disputed among Sorrento, Amalfi and Capri, and the liqueur was long a homemade drink of the south before firms such as Pallini bottled it for sale across Italy and abroad.
villamassalimoncello-sb: Villa Massa is a Sorrento limoncello made by the Massa family, who turned a family recipe into a commercial brand in the early 1990s, as limoncello was spreading from southern Italian homes to bars far beyond. It is made from Sorrento lemons, the Ovale di Sorrento with its thick, fragrant peel, protected under the Limone di Sorrento name, steeped in alcohol and sweetened. Sorrento, Amalfi and Capri all claim to be limoncello's birthplace.
disaronno-sb: Disaronno's makers date it to 1525 and tell a legend: the painter Bernardino Luini, decorating a church in Saronno with a fresco of the Madonna, was given a liqueur by the young widow who modelled for him. The documented business belongs to the Reina family of Saronno, whose company, Illva Saronno, made it famous as Amaretto di Saronno before renaming it Disaronno Originale in 2001. Despite its almond flavour it contains no almonds, relying instead on apricot kernel oil, herbs and fruits.
lazzaroniamaretto-sb: Lazzaroni is a Saronno family company best known for its amaretti di Saronno, the crisp almond and apricot-kernel biscuits sold in red tins, and its amaretto liqueur is made by infusing those biscuits in alcohol rather than relying on kernel oil alone. The family dates its liqueur to 1851. Saronno, a town north of Milan, gives its name to the whole amaretto tradition, and Lazzaroni's is one of the town's two historic amarettos, alongside Disaronno.
nocinosibona-sb: Nocino is a dark liqueur of unripe green walnuts, steeped with sugar and spices in alcohol for weeks, and tradition, especially around Modena in Emilia-Romagna, says the walnuts must be picked on or around the night of St John, 24 June, while their shells are still soft. Families made it at home each summer to open in winter. Sibona, a Piedmontese distillery at Piobesi d'Alba better known for grappa, bottles a commercial nocino in that tradition.
gallianolautentico-sb: Galliano was created in 1896 by Arturo Vaccari, a distiller in Livorno, Tuscany, who named it after Giuseppe Galliano, an Italian army officer celebrated for his defence of a fort at Mekele during the First Italo-Ethiopian War. Its vanilla and anise flavour, golden colour and tall bottle shaped like a classical column made it distinctive, and in the 1970s it became famous in the United States through the Harvey Wallbanger. Its owner, Lucas Bols, presents L'Autentico as a return to the original strength and recipe.
sambucaromana-sb: Sambuca is the anise liqueur of Lazio, and its commercial history begins in the port of Civitavecchia in the mid-nineteenth century, when Luigi Manzi sold an anise liqueur under that name. The word is usually traced to the Latin for elder, sambucus, though other derivations have been proposed. Sambuca Romana takes its name from Rome and is one of the brands that carried the liqueur abroad; it is often served con la mosca, with coffee beans floating in the glass.
molinarisambucaextra-sb: Angelo Molinari began making his Sambuca Extra in Civitavecchia, the port north of Rome, in 1945, in the town where Luigi Manzi had sold the first commercial sambuca nearly a century earlier, and his brand helped make sambuca a national drink in post-war Italy. Molinari's Extra is a clear anise liqueur made with star anise and other aromatics. It is often served con la mosca, with three coffee beans floating in the glass.
tiamaria-sb: Tia Maria was developed in Jamaica in 1946 by Dr Ken Evans, working with Morris Cargill, who wanted a coffee liqueur like the one his aunt had made. Brand lore long told of a colonial-era recipe saved by a maid, but by Cargill's account he never got his aunt's recipe, and a partner suggested naming the liqueur after her: Aunt Mary, Tia Maria. Illva Saronno, makers of Disaronno, bought the brand from Pernod Ricard in 2009.
mrblack-sb: Mr Black was launched in 2013 in New South Wales, Australia, by the distiller Tom Baker and the designer Philip Moore, who wanted a coffee liqueur that tasted chiefly of coffee rather than of sugar. It is made from cold-brewed specialty coffee blended with Australian vodka, with far less sweetness than older coffee liqueurs, and it was developed with Australia's café culture and the espresso martini in mind before spreading to bars abroad.
baileysirishcream-sb: Baileys was launched in 1974 by Gilbeys of Ireland, part of International Distillers and Vintners, as the first Irish cream liqueur. The idea came from a London team, Tom Jago, David Gluckman and Hugh Seymour-Davies, asked to create a new drink for Ireland; combining Irish whiskey with fresh Irish cream also made use of surplus dairy cream. By its creators' account the name was borrowed from a restaurant near their office in Soho, and the R. A. Bailey signature on the label belongs to no real person.
carolans-sb: Carolans was developed in Ireland in 1978 and first sold in the UK in 1979, one of the earliest rivals to Baileys in the Irish cream category Baileys had created only a few years before. It blends Irish spirits and whiskey with cream and honey, the honey being its distinguishing note. After passing through several owners, among them William Grant and Campari, it was bought by Heaven Hill in 2017.
advocaatwarninks-sb: Advocaat's commercial history is usually dated to 1828, when J. G. Cooymans began making an egg liqueur at his distillery in 's-Hertogenbosch, though its origins are disputed. One theory links it to an avocado drink Dutch colonists met in Brazil, with egg yolk replacing the avocado back home; another derives the name from advocatenborrel, a lawyers' drink. Warninks became one of the best-known Dutch brands of this thick egg liqueur, traditionally eaten with a spoon.
verpoorteneierlikor-sb: Verpoorten was founded in 1876 by Eugen Verpoorten, who opened a liquor and colonial goods business in Heinsberg, in the German Rhineland, and began making an egg liqueur. The firm moved to Berlin in 1920 and, after the Second World War, to Bonn, where it has been based since 1952. It is still family-owned, now in its fifth generation, and the company says its recipe of egg yolks, sugar and spirit has not changed since the start.
velvetfalernum-sb: Falernum is a Barbadian syrup liqueur of rum, lime, ginger, clove and almond, made on the island since at least the nineteenth century; its name may echo the Falernian wine of ancient Rome, though other stories exist. John D. Taylor's Velvet Falernum, which the brand dates to 1890, took its name from the syrup's thick, velvety texture and became the best-known commercial version. It is now produced in Barbados by R. L. Seale and appears in tiki drinks such as the Zombie.
stelizabethallspicedram-sb: Allspice dram, also called pimento dram, is a Jamaican liqueur of rum infused with the dried berries of the pimento tree, which grows on the island and is what the English-speaking world calls allspice. Tiki bartenders of the mid-twentieth century used it in their recipes, but it later vanished from most bars outside Jamaica. This bottling is named after St Elizabeth, a parish in southwest Jamaica, and its arrival in the US in the late 2000s let bartenders make those recipes again.
choyaumeshu-sb: Choya began in 1914 with grape growing in Habikino, near Osaka, and the company was founded in 1924 to make wine. In 1959 it began making umeshu, the Japanese liqueur of green ume fruit steeped in spirit with sugar, which households had long made at home each June when the fruit ripens. Ume is usually called a plum in English but is closer to an apricot, and many of the company's bottles carry whole ume fruit inside.
takaraplumwine-sb: Takara is the Kyoto drinks company whose roots go back to 1842 in Fushimi, a district famous for its sake breweries, and which grew into one of Japan's largest makers of sake, shochu and mirin. Its plum wine follows the Japanese tradition of ume, a sour fruit related to the apricot, used to make a sweet, tart drink; strictly, umeshu is ume steeped in spirit, while plum wine is a broader term. Takara also owns the Tomatin whisky distillery in Scotland.
archerspeachschnapps-sb: Archers Peach Schnapps arrived in Britain in the late 1980s, during the fashion for sweet, fruity schnapps that followed the success of peach schnapps in the United States, and it became a fixture of British bars. It is a clear, sweet peach liqueur rather than a schnapps in the German sense of a fruit brandy, and it found its way into simple long drinks such as the Woo Woo and the Sex on the Beach.
dekuyperpeachtree-sb: De Kuyper Peachtree was introduced in the US in the mid-1980s and touched off the peach schnapps boom, inspiring drinks such as the Fuzzy Navel, peach schnapps with orange juice. The De Kuyper family business began in 1695, when Petrus De Kuyper started making casks in the Netherlands, and by 1752 the family ran a distillery in Schiedam, the centre of Dutch genever. In America the brand had been made under licence since the end of Prohibition, and the company became De Kuyper Royal Distillers in 1995.
midori-sb: Suntory first sold its melon liqueur in Japan in 1964 as Hermes Melon Liqueur, and in 1978 renamed it Midori, Japanese for green, for its American debut at a party at Studio 54 in New York celebrating the film Saturday Night Fever. Its bright colour suited the cocktail fashions of the following decade, notably the Japanese Slipper, created in Melbourne. In 2013 Suntory reformulated it with less sugar and moved it to a frosted bottle. It is flavoured with Japanese melons, including the Yubari King.
cointreaubloodorange-sb: Cointreau Blood Orange is a variation on the orange liqueur the Cointreau family first sold in 1875 in Angers, made by adding the peel of blood oranges, with their berry-like edge, to the house's blend of sweet and bitter orange peels. The original Cointreau is credited to Édouard Cointreau, whose father and uncle, both confectioners, had founded the family distillery in 1849. Rémy Cointreau, formed when Cointreau merged with Rémy Martin in 1990, makes both at Saint-Barthélemy-d'Anjou, just outside Angers.
sheridans-sb: Sheridan's went on sale in 1994 in a bottle split into two chambers, one holding a dark coffee and whiskey liqueur and the other a white vanilla cream, poured together so the two settle in the glass. The idea came from Pat Rigney, head of research and development for Baileys, who first conceived it in the 1980s, and it is made in Dublin under the name of Thomas Sheridan and Sons. It was part of the wave of Irish cream liqueurs that followed Baileys.
benedictinedom-sb: Bénédictine was created in 1863 by Alexandre Le Grand, a wine merchant in Fécamp, Normandy, who worked with a local chemist from old herbal formulas. He promoted it with a story that it revived a recipe of the Benedictine monks of Fécamp Abbey, attributed to a monk named Dom Bernardo Vincelli in 1510, a tale historians regard as marketing. The D.O.M. on the label stands for Deo Optimo Maximo, to God, most good, most great. Le Grand commissioned the ornate Palais Bénédictine in Fécamp, where it is still made.
izarraverte-sb: Izarra was created in 1906 by Joseph Grattau, a botanist and pharmacist, in Hendaye in the French Basque Country, and its name is the Basque word for star. In 1912 the business opened a large distillery in Bayonne on the banks of the Adour, which operated there until 1998. Green Izarra is made from seventeen plants and spices, distilled and blended with armagnac and bottled at 48 per cent, while the yellow version is softer, at 40.
genepilechamois-sb: Génépi is the Alpine liqueur of Savoie and the Aosta Valley, made from small, silvery artemisia plants, relatives of wormwood, that grow above the treeline, and its name is the local word for the plants themselves. Mountain families once gathered the wild plants in late summer and steeped them in spirit with sugar at home; today most génépi uses cultivated plants, because wild picking is restricted. Le Chamois takes its name from the chamois, the Alpine goat-antelope.
mastihaskinos-sb: Mastiha liqueur is flavoured with the resin of the mastic tree, which is harvested as tear-like drops only in the south of Chios, in the island's mastic villages, and has been traded since antiquity; Chios mastic is a protected product, and Chios mastiha liqueur has its own geographical indication. Skinos was launched as a modern brand of mastiha liqueur for bars and export, and its name is the Greek word for the mastic tree. It is a clear, piney, faintly sweet spirit.
beerenburgsonnema-sb: Beerenburg takes its name from Hendrik Beerenburg, an Amsterdam spice merchant who opened a shop on the Stromarkt in 1724 and sold a herb mix for steeping in genever. The habit caught on far more in the northern provinces of Friesland, Groningen and Drenthe than in Amsterdam, and Frisian distillers took the drink up as their own. Sonnema, from Dokkum in Friesland, is one of the best-known of them, making a herbal genever bitter with gentian, bay leaf and other botanicals.
zirbenzstonepine-sb: Zirbenschnaps is an Alpine tradition from Austria and South Tyrol: young cones of the Swiss stone pine, the Zirbe, are picked green in early summer and steeped in spirit, which turns red-brown and takes on a resinous, piney flavour. Families made it at home and mountain inns served their own. Zirbenz is a commercial version, made in Austria from the cones of high Alpine trees and brought to the American market by the importer Haus Alpenz.
enziangrassl-sb: Grassl was founded in 1602 at Berchtesgaden, in the Bavarian Alps, and is regarded as Germany's oldest gentian distillery. It holds rights to dig the roots of yellow gentian on mountain pastures that now lie within the Berchtesgaden National Park, and the roots are traditionally distilled in small huts up on the mountain before the spirit is brought down. Enzian, German for gentian, is a clear, earthy, bitter spirit distilled from the fermented roots rather than flavoured with them.
hierbasibicencas-sb: Hierbas Ibicencas is the herbal liqueur of Ibiza, made by steeping local plants such as thyme, rosemary, fennel, lemon verbena and juniper in an anise spirit, and islanders made it at home for generations, each family with its own blend. It is now a protected geographical indication, and sprigs of the herbs are often left in the bottle. The island's commercial producers bottle versions of that household recipe, and it is usually served cold after a meal.
travaricabadel-sb: Travarica, from trava, herb, is the herbal rakija of Croatia's Adriatic coast, especially Dalmatia, where grape brandy is steeped with local plants such as sage, rue, fennel, mint and carob, and families made it at home from their own grape spirit. Badel, the Zagreb drinks company that counts 1862 as its beginning and carries the date in its name, bottles a commercial travarica in that tradition. The company took its modern shape after the Second World War from several older firms.
brancamenta-sb: Fratelli Branca introduced Branca Menta in the 1960s as a sweeter, mint-flavoured companion to Fernet-Branca, the bitter that Bernardino Branca, a self-taught herbalist, created in Milan in 1845 and sold with his sons. One story told about it is that the opera singer Maria Callas suggested adding mint to fernet. It keeps the bitter herbal base of the original, with peppermint oil added, and is still made in Milan by the Branca family company.
amarosfumatorabarbaro-sb: Amaro Sfumato Rabarbaro comes from Cappelletti, a family firm in Aldeno, in Trentino in the Italian Alps, founded in 1909 by Giuseppe Cappelletti and also known for its wine-based aperitivo. Rabarbaro amari, flavoured with Chinese rhubarb root, are an old northern Italian style, and Sfumato, smoky, takes its name from the smoky edge that sets it apart from other rhubarb bitters. It is made from rhubarb, alpine herbs and sugar on a spirit base, and is drunk as an after-dinner amaro.
amarobraulio-sb: Amaro Braulio was first sold commercially in 1875 by Francesco Peloni, a pharmacist in Bormio, in the Valtellina high in the Lombard Alps, working from a recipe of mountain herbs, roots and berries such as gentian, juniper and wormwood. It takes its name from the Braulio, the mountain and valley above the town, and it is still made at the Peloni family's premises in Bormio, where it is aged for two years in Slavonian oak casks.
melettiamaro-sb: Meletti is the family firm Silvio Meletti founded in Ascoli Piceno, in the Marche, in 1870, first to make an anise liqueur, the Anisetta Meletti that remains its best-known product. The family also gave its name to the Caffè Meletti on the city's Piazza del Popolo, an elegant café that became a local landmark. Its amaro, built on herbs, spices and citrus with a light, floral character, came later, and the company is still run by Meletti descendants.
pelinkovacbadel-sb: Pelinkovac takes its name from pelin, wormwood, the bitter herb at its heart, and it is a dark, bittersweet liqueur long popular in Croatia, Slovenia and Serbia, where it is drunk as an aperitif or after a meal. Badel, the Zagreb drinks company that counts 1862 as its beginning, is today one of its best-known producers, making it from wormwood and other herbs macerated in spirit and sweetened. The company took shape after the Second World War from several older Zagreb firms.
pernodabsinthe-sb: Henri-Louis Pernod founded his absinthe distillery at Pontarlier, near the Swiss border, in 1805, after starting in Couvet, Switzerland, in 1797 with a recipe linked to Dr Pierre Ordinaire, and Pernod Fils became the most prestigious absinthe of the Belle Époque. France banned absinthe in 1915 and the company turned to anise. After the European bans were lifted, Pernod brought absinthe back, and in 2013 it reformulated it to come closer to the pre-1915 recipe, with a grape spirit base.
lafeeparisienne-sb: La Fée, the fairy, was launched at the end of the 1990s by the British entrepreneur George Rowley, working with the French absinthe historian Marie-Claude Delahaye, founder of an absinthe museum at Auvers-sur-Oise, as absinthe began to return to European shelves. Its name recalls la fée verte, the green fairy, the nickname absinthe earned in nineteenth-century Paris, and its eye logo became a familiar emblem of the revival. The Parisienne is the brand's classic green absinthe, made in France.
stgeorgeabsintheverte-sb: St. George Absinthe Verte was released at the end of the 2000s, after US regulators began approving absinthe again, making it one of the first absinthes legally made in the United States since the ban of 1912. Its creator, Lance Winters, St. George's master distiller, had been working on the recipe for some eleven years. St. George Spirits itself, now based in Alameda, California, was founded in 1982 by the German-born Jörg Rupf, who began by making fruit brandies in the European manner.
ricard-sb: Paul Ricard, a Marseille native, launched his pastis in 1932, billing it as the real pastis of Marseille, in the space absinthe had left after it was banned in 1915. His anise and liquorice aperitif, diluted with cold water until it turns cloudy, became one of France's most popular drinks. The Vichy regime banned pastis during the war, and it returned at full strength only in 1951. In 1975 Ricard merged with its old rival Pernod to form Pernod Ricard.
pernodanise-sb: Pernod's anise grew out of the absinthe house Henri-Louis Pernod founded at Pontarlier in 1805. When France banned absinthe in 1915, the company turned to an aniseed spirit made without wormwood, and that drink, bottled at a lower strength than its predecessor, became Pernod as most drinkers now know it. It is a pale yellow-green and turns cloudy with water. In 1975 the company merged with its great Marseille rival, Ricard, to create Pernod Ricard.
henribardouinpastis-sb: Henri Bardouin is made by Distilleries et Domaines de Provence in Forcalquier, in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence, a house that dates itself to 1898 and is known for liqueurs and aperitifs drawn from the plants of the surrounding hills. Its pastis is unusually complex for the style, built from dozens of herbs and spices beyond anise and liquorice, many of them from Haute-Provence. Pastis became the classic aperitif of southern France after absinthe was banned in 1915.
ouzo12-sb: Ouzo 12 was first made in 1880 by the Kaloyannis brothers, distillers in Constantinople, and its name, the story goes, comes from the cask customers liked best, number 12, which the brothers then used for the whole brand. It went on to become one of the best-known ouzos in Greece. Ouzo is a protected name reserved for Greece and Cyprus, and the origin of the word itself is disputed, between an Italian shipping mark, uso Marsiglia, and the Turkish word for grape.
ouzoplomari-sb: Ouzo Plomari was first distilled in 1894 by Isidoros Arvanitis in Plomari, a harbour town on the island of Lesbos that is one of the most celebrated homes of ouzo, and it carries the town's name. Lesbos has a long ouzo tradition built on local aniseed, and Plomari's distilleries made the town's name a byword for the spirit across Greece. Ouzo itself is a protected name that may only be used for spirits made in Greece and Cyprus.
yenirak-sb: Yeni Rakı was introduced in 1937 by Tekel, the Turkish state monopoly on alcohol and tobacco, and the state went on making it for nearly seven decades. Its name means new rakı. Rakı is an aniseed spirit that turns milky white when water is added, which is why Turks call it lion's milk, and it is traditionally served with meze. When Tekel's spirits business was privatised in 2004, Mey İçki took over the brand, and Diageo bought Mey in 2011.
